div.p: Despite the advancements in supporting artificial intelligence, accelerator-enabled computing architectures still struggle to meet strict timing constraints due to the complex interactions between CPU cores and accelerators. Although various scheduling and response-time analysis techniques have been developed, a significant gap remains between the conservative hard real-time schedulability (i.e., worst-case response times) and the average measured schedulability on real systems. This pessimism significantly limits the deployment of hard real-time tasks on accelerator-enabled computing platforms.

To address this, we propose HARD, a real-time scheduling approach that integrates scheduling strategies, response time analysis, and practical scheduler designs for general acceleratorenabled computing platforms. Benefiting the subtask level segmented characteristics that are ignored by classic schedulers, the proposed HARD can significantly improve the theoretically guaranteed hard real-time schedulability. Extensive experiments on off-the-shelf Intel CPUs and NVIDIA GPUs show that HARD outperforms state-of-the-art scheduling and analysis approaches, delivering a 11.3% improvement in hard real-time schedulability and a remarkable 45.1% reduction in pessimism.

Index Terms-Heterogeneous Architecture, Accelerator, Realtime Scheduling, Response Time Analysis 1 A theoretically guaranteed pseudopolynomial-time analysis (HRT) of Rate Monotonic scheduling and an AMS with setup details in Sec. VI.
389 2025 IEEE 31st Real-Time and Embedded Technology and Applications Symposium (RTAS)

div.head: I. INTRODUCTION
div.p: To address the demanding computational requirements posed by sophisticated computation tasks, especially Artificial Intelligence (AI) applications, computing architectures designed for embedded or cloud-based scenarios are increasingly embracing accelerators [1], [2]. These architectures seamlessly integrate multiple CPU cores that are used for central control with the accelerators that incorporate many Processing Elements (PEs), such as GPU Streaming Multiprocessors (SMs) and FPGA IP cores [3]. On the accelerator-enabled computing platforms, computation tasks include both CPU and accelerator workloads. These tasks are initially executed on the CPU and subsequently offloaded to the accelerators, behaving in a segmented manner and creating multiple rounds of dynamic interplay between the CPU and the accelerators [4], [5]. The interleaved and complicated task execution manner leads to the challenges of scheduling the computation tasks, especially under real-time constraints [6].

Hard real-time (HRT) tasks have stringent deadlines that must be met; failure to do so can result in catastrophic § Corresponding author. This work is supported by NSFC 62202287. consequences. However, on accelerator-enabled heterogeneous platforms, the schedulability of HRT tasks-derived from theoretical response times-often lags significantly behind the average measured schedulability (AMS), which is observed in runtime on actual accelerator-enabled computing systems. This gap is known as pessimism. To illustrate the pessimism, Fig. 1 highlights that considerable pessimism universally happens in using the classic Rate-Monotonic scheduler 1 .

Today's mainstream real-time scheduling and responsetime analysis methods-such as deadline-driven [6], [7] and priority-driven [8], [9] approaches-are originally developed for the system with multiple CPU cores, primarily based on task-level features. They fail to capture the complex, interleaved execution patterns on the accelerator-enabled platforms, which occur at finer granularities.

Targeting the features of accelerator-enabled platforms, we propose HARD, a novel real-time scheduling approach. HARD leverages subtask-level timeslot allocation with userdefinable granularity, aligning naturally with the segmented characteristics. The primary goals of the HARD are threefold: (1) Improve the schedulability for HRT, i.e., increasing utilization across different schedulable ratios in theoretical response time analysis. (2) Maintain or even improve the AMS, i.e., maintaining or increasing utilization across different schedulable ratios in the measurements on the real system. (3) Ensure the practicality of the proposed approach which can work as a runtime plug-in module and be easily applied to off-the-shelf accelerator-based computing systems.
The contributions of this work are four-fold:

• Extracting common features and building task execution models on accelerator-enabled computing architectures, we present a scheduling strategy by timeslot allocation, which is optimized through dynamic programming.

• Deriving a tight theoretical response time analysis under timeslot allocation, our approach improves HRT schedulability for accelerator-based computing architectures. • Developing a practical real-time scheduler for the timeslot allocation in the operating system, we design fine-grained time tracing in kernel modules and then achieve the scheduling at user-definable granularity. • Conducting extensive numerical and real system experiments, we demonstrate the proposed approach can improve HRT schedulability by 11.3%, AMS schedulability by 2.9%, and reduce pessimism by 45.1%. The remainder of the article is organized as follows. Secs. II and III present the background and modeling for the accelerator-enabled computing architecture. Sec. IV introduces the time allocation and its response time analysis. Sec. V describes the development of the real-time scheduler in the operating system. Sec. VI discusses the extensive numerical and real system experiments. Secs. II-C and VII review and conclude this paper.

div.head: II. BACKGROUND A. Accelerator-Enabled Architecture and Segmented Model
div.p: Accelerator-enabled computing platforms, characterized by the integration of general-purpose CPU processors with multiple accelerators, such as GPUs, TPUs, DSPs or FPGAs, are increasingly adopted in both embedded computing, exemplified by the NVIDIA Jetson Series [10], and enterprise-grade singlenode servers featuring powerful GPUs (e.g., HPE ProLiant Series with integrated accelerators [11]). Typically, in the execution of applications on accelerator-based computing platforms, the CPU handles I/O operations and serial computation, while parallel executions are delegated to the accelerators [12], [13]. The execution of tasks on such architectures follows an interleaved pattern -generally, the tasks predominantly utilize CPU cores for serial computation but can concurrently engage multiple PEs within the accelerator for parallel computation to optimize the overall computational process [14]- [16].

One of the task models for the heterogeneous architecture is Multi-Segment Self-Suspension (MSSS) model [7], [17], [18]. In this model, a task τ i consists of m i execution segments and m i -1 suspension segments between the execution segments. Thus, a task τ i with deadline D i and period T i is expressed as a 3-tuple:
div.formula: τi = (L 0 i , S 0 i , L 1 i , ..., S m i -2 i , L m i -1 i ), Di, Ti ,(1)
div.p: where L j i and S j i are the lengths of the j + 1-th execution and suspension segments, respectively. From the CPU perspective, L j i s are the workload on CPUs, while S j i s are the workload offloaded to the PEs, behaving like suspension intervals.

div.head: B. The Pessimism in Accelerator Enabled Computing
div.p: Hard real-time (HRT) tasks, such as autonomous driving [19] and drone control [20], impose stringent timing constraints to guarantee system accuracy and safety. They requires rigorous theoretical response time analysis and schedulability guarantees for real-time tasks, even under worst-case conditions. There is a gap between the schedulability from theoretical response time analysis which considers the worst case and the average measured schedulability on real systems. This gap is called pessimism. It not only incorporates worstcase scenarios, such as worst-case execution time but also arises from non-ideal response time analysis. As computing architectures become more complex, the pessimism is more serious, limiting computing performance for HRT tasks [4], [18]. As reported by related works in Sec.II-C, the gap (pessimism) can be as large as half of the total schedulability.

div.head: C. Related Works
div.p: Early studies on real-time scheduling for accelerators, such as GPUs, treated them as non-preemptive entities [23]- [25]. Recently, researchers have added preemption [26], [27] and partitioning functions [28], [29]. For instance, Park et al. [30], Tanasic et al. [31], and Zhou et al. [32] proposed architecture extensions to improve preemption, tested on GPU simulators. The Effisha framework [33] introduced software techniques for kernel preemption. Yalcinkaya et al. [22] mapped the schedulability problem to the reachability problem in timed automata for self-suspension tasks with fixed preemption points. Capodieci [34] introduced a real-time scheduler for GPUs in automotive-grade embedded systems, leveraging preemption capabilities such as pixel and thread-level preemption on NVIDIA GPUs. Partitioning also supports flexible task execution on PEs with low design costs [28], now officially supported by state-of-the-art GPUs [29].

Alongside the system improvements, Huang et al. [17] presented a scheduling algorithm and response time analysis for uni-core CPU-based architectures using the MSSS model. Saha et al. [4] introduced a spatial-temporal scheduling solution for GPUs. Xu et al. [9] proposed a scheduling algorithm for multi-core CPU-based architectures. Zou et al. [5] developed a scheduling mechanism for heterogeneous systems. Patel et al. [35] extended MPCP schedulability analysis using the MSSS model. Günzel proposed a suspension-aware analysis on uniprocessor EDF-like scheduling [7]. Besides response time analysis frameworks, researchers also delved deeper into providing OS-integrated scheduling design for accelerator computing systems. TimeGraph [36] was an event-driven GPU scheduler at the device-driver level designed to prioritize GPU workloads, maintaining frame rates for critical tasks with minimal overhead. Chen et al. [37] proposed a runtime system orchestrating parallel computing tasks to accelerator hardware utilization. Prophet [38] predicted performance degradation in latency-sensitive applications, allowing for improved colocation decisions while maintaining QoS. Batchmaker [39] by Gao et al. focused on cellular batching of RNN to optimize both latency and throughput during inference.

A close examination of related works (as shown in Tbl. I) reveals common challenges for real-time computing on accelerator-based architectures: (1) Many studies focus on one CPU core and many PEs, with few considering the practical co-existence of multiple CPUs. (2) Response time analysis is time-consuming to derive and overly pessimistic for classic real-time schedulers. (3) Providing strict response time analysis for heuristic scheduling approaches is challenging. (4) There is a lack of fine-grained OS scheduling and response time analysis co-design to provide both runtime measured schedulability and tight, easy-to-obtain response time analysis with HRT performance.

To address these challenges, this paper introduces a novel real-time scheduling approach HARD, which leverages subtask-level timeslot allocation with user-definable granularity. By leveraging the sub-task level segmented characteristics, it significantly enhances the HRT schedulability and minimizes pessimism.

div.head: III. SYSTEM FEATURE AND MODEL NOTATIONS
div.p: Following the background, Sec. III-A presents the common features of the hardware architecture, and Sec. III-B introduces the model and notations. The following scheduling methodologies are built on the models described in this section.

div.head: A. Features of Targeted Computing Architecture
div.p: Given a general accelerator-enabled computing architecture, introduced in Sec. II.A, there are N CP U CPU cores and N P E accelerator processing elements (PEs). The mainstream CPU cores, such as X86, ARM, and RISC-V, support preemptive execution mode. Since CPU workloads primarily handle I/O and control tasks with infrequent parallel operations, each CPU workload is executed on one core [40], [41].

Accelerators, such as GPUs with their PEs (streaming multiprocessors) [42], have partitionable architectures, allowing workloads to be executed in parallel across multiple PEs. Without loss of generality, this paper targets the accelerators with multiple task partitions, supported by modern commercial products such as NVIDIA Ampere architecture [29] and FPGA IP cores [28]. In addition to the multiple task partitions explored in this work, preemption is also a possible architectural approach to improve the flexibility of accelerators [43], which we will study in future works. The real-time tasks are managed by the operating system's scheduler and dynamically executed on the processors. As the OS runs on the CPU cores, which support preemptive multitasking with fine granularity, the CPU workloads are scheduled by the OS scheduler. In contrast, the accelerator, designed for extreme computational efficiency, functions like a peripheral device. When a workload is being dispatched to the accelerator, it inherits the task's priority. Once the workload reaches the accelerator, it operates on a first-come, first-served basis unless a specific scheduler is implemented within the accelerator. The key features of the targeted computing architecture are presented in Tbl. II. Our modeling and scheduling-real-time scheduling of the workloads across processor cores-lies on the above-discussed architecture and its modeling parameters are listed in Tbl. III. We will explain these parameters as we develop our models in Sec. III-B.

div.head: B. Task Model and Notations
div.p: A set of n independent parallel real-time tasks τ = {τ 0 , τ 1 , ..., τ n-1 } are executed on the accelerator-enabled computing architecture. After the compiling and resource mapping (performed by research framework like CEDR [44], SOSPCS [45], or commercialized compiler like NVCC [46] etc.), a task is made up of several segmented workloads. Each task τ i comprises m i CPU workloads separated by m i-1 PE workloads, with a deadline D i and release period T i . Note that for multi-accelerator systems, the same PE workloads may exhibit different lengths when executing on different accelerators. But they strictly follow the temporal order: a CPU workload becomes eligible for execution only after the completion of its preceding PE workload, and vice versa. Thus, task τ i can be characterized by the 3-tuple:
div.formula: τi = (CL 0 i , P L 0 i , CL 1 i , ..., P L m i -2 i , CL m i -1 i ), Ti, Di ,(2)
div.p: where CL j i and P L j i denote the execution times of the (j +1)th CPU workload and PE workload, respectively, in task τ i . All execution times are non-zero integers. Each task has a priority π i , which is consequently inherited by the task's CPU and PE workloads.

The PE workloads are partitioned across dedicated groups of PEs at the compile stage, minimizing interference between tasks. We incorporate the time for copying data between CPUs and PEs into the total PE execution time [47], [48].
Given N P E homogeneous PEs, the execution time P T of PE workload P L follows the Amdahl and Gustafson's law [49]:
div.formula: P T = P L (1 -p) + NP E × p ,(3)
div.p: where p represents the parallelizable portion of the workload, and 1 -p accounts for serial execution, such as copying data from CPU cores to PEs. The partitioning ensures minor contention or interference between concurrently executing tasks, mitigating resource contention impacts on WCET.

The task parameters, such as CL, P L, and p for each workload, can be profiled in advance by measuring their worst case execution times. For specific applications, the task parameters are offered by the algorithm developers such as autonomous driving [50]. As these parameters are derived from the measured execution times, the uncertainties at lower microarchitecture levels, such as cache misses, are naturally encompassed within the task parameters.

div.head: IV. LIGHT-WEIGHT SCHEDULING STRATEGY AND CORRESPONDING RESPONSE TIME ANALYSIS
div.p: Following the task model and the interleaved task execution pattern, we first make an overview on the response time of an entire task in Sec. IV-A. Then, we coordinate our scheduling strategy and response time analysis for the realtime performance for CPU and PE workloads in Sec. IV-B and Sec. IV-C, respectively. Finally, an end-to-end scheduling approach is provided in Sec. IV-D.

div.head: A. Overview of the Task Response Time
div.p: Based on the targeted architecture and its task model in Sec. III, the response time of task τ i equals the sum of each workload's response time:
div.formula: Theorem IV.1 Response time of task τ i Ri = CR 0 i + P R 0 i + • • • + P R m i -2 i + CR m i -1 i ,(4)
div.p: where CR j i and P R j i are the response time of CL j i and P L j i , respectively.
PROOF. 1 Due to the task workload temporal dependency, the response time of the whole task can be broken down to workload level on CPUs and PEs. □
For response time analysis, the scheduling is feasible if and only if the theoretical response time of all the tasks are less or equal to their deadlines, i.e., R i ≤ D i , ∀i ∈ {0, 1 . . . , n -1}.

In the following, we build the scheduling strategy and analyze response time CR j i and P R j i for each task. B. Scheduling and Response Time of CPU Workloads 1) Motivation -Response Time Considerations: We outline a general response time function f , which captures the importance of analyzing CPU workloads in accelerator-enabled computing systems.
div.formula: CR j i = f πi, CL j i , NCP U , (uc0, uc1, . . . , ucn-1) .(5)
div.p: The response time CR j i is modeled as a function of the task priority π i , workload length CL j i , the number of processors N CP U , and the utilization contributed by CPU workloads {uc i } as shown in Eqn. (5). Followings are general considerations and requirements for such a function:

• The returned value is inversely correlated with π i and N CP U ; and positively correlated with CL j i and {uc i }; • The expression of f should be as concise as possible to reduce the pessimism of the analysis. Scheduling and timing analysis of CPU workloads is critical, as it not only affects the CPU tasks themselves but also determines the release of subsequent PE workloads. To address the granularity issues of traditional deadline-driven or prioritydriven scheduling at the task level and to enable response time analysis through simple and elegant formulas, we propose a dynamic timeslot allocation strategy. This strategy considers all the parameters defined in the function f , enabling accurate and fine-granularity control over CPU workload execution.

Let's start with a fair timeslot allocation strategy [51], as illustrated in Fig. 2a. We assume five tasks, τ 0 through τ 4 , are running on two CPUs. The scheduler cycles through five rounds before the scheduling pattern repeats, scheduling each task twice per cycle. Therefore, for a CPU workload CL j i , we can bound its response time by ⌈CL j i /2⌉ × 5. Lemma IV.2 Response time of fair timeslot allocation
div.formula: CR j i ≤ CL j i NCP U × n, (6
div.p: where n is the number of tasks.

PROOF. 2 The scheduler cycles through the tasks, giving each a fixed time slice (1 time unit). In each n-unit round, a task is scheduled N CP U times. To schedule task τ i for at least CL j i time units, the scheduler cycles at most CL j i /N CP U rounds. Pessimism occurs when CL j i is not divisible by N CP U , leading to an extra round even if fewer executions are needed to complete the workload. □

As shown in Lemma IV.2, the response time of the fairshare strategy is straightforward to analyze with acceptable pessimism. However, due to its strict timing fairness, this schedule sacrifices tasks with higher utilization (i.e., tighter deadlines) while benefiting lower-utilization tasks. To increase schedulability while maintaining analytical simplicity, we assign different timeslots to each task, presenting a dynamic timeslot allocating based on the task properties. Fig. 2b demonstrates the response time analysis under a heuristically adjusted timeslot allocation. Assume tasks are sorted by Rate-Monotonic order, τ 0 through τ 4 . For τ 0 and τ 1 , which release more frequently and are more likely to fail the system, we assign more timeslots (w 0 = w 1 = 3). Less slots are assigned for the other three tasks (w 2 = w 3 = w 4 = 2). Their theoretical response time changes accordingly. For a CPU workload CL j i , where i = 0, 1 we can bound its response time by ⌈CL j i /3⌉ × 6 because τ 0 and τ 1 are scheduled three times in six units periodically.

Using the same benchmarks as in Fig. 1, we evaluate the system response time using Theorem IV.1 and compare the scheduling performance of the fair allocation and heuristically adjusted allocation (the scheduling and response time analysis of PEs are referred to Sec. IV.C). Fig. 2c demonstrates that even the heuristically assigned slots above can effectively increase system performance (measured by the area under the curve) by 8.20% and 8.24%, respectively.
2) Theory -Response Time for Timeslot Allocation: Extending Lemma IV.2, the response time of the adjusted timeslot allocation can be calculated in Theorem IV.3.

div.head: Theorem IV.3
div.p: Response time for allocating w 0 , w 1 , . . . , w n-1 slots for each task respectively,
div.formula: CR j i ≤ CL j i wi × i wi NCP U = CL j i wi × S,(7)
div.p: where S is the scheduling window defined by
div.formula: S := ( n-1 i=0 wi)/NCP U .(8)
div.p: PROOF. 3 The scheduler cycles through all tasks, and each cycle takes S time units, during which each task is scheduled w i times. The scheduler cycles at most CL j i /w i rounds. □
The pessimism arises when CL j i is not a multiple of w i . In the worst case, when CL j i = k × w i + 1, the entire period must be paid for the last slice, which worsens as S increases.
To reduce pessimism, we need to consider the response time for workloads whose lengths are less than S.
Corollary IV.3.1 A tighter bound for workload response time with w i slots allocated to τ i :
div.formula: CR j i ≤ k × S + CRi(r),(9)
div.p: where CL j i = k × w i + r by Euclidean Division and CR i (r) denotes the response time for the residual workload of task τ i , length r.

PROOF. 4 The scheduler needs to cycle k rounds, each taking S time units. For the remainder, we check the response time at every tick over the whole window to find the worst case response time. A case study is illustrated in Fig. 3. □

3) Procedure -Towards Optimal Slot Allocation: Such motivation leads us to find the optimal number of slots w i for each task to improve the system's schedulability. Through the process, two key questions emerge: 1 Since running full scheduling experiments for each allocation is time-consuming, how can we efficiently evaluate the allocation? 2 Under these evaluation metrics, what algorithms can be adopted to find the optimal slot allocation effectively? To address question 1 , we consider that one of our design objectives in Sec. IV-B is to meet the deadlines of each task, as the penalty for system failure due to any task missing is the same. Therefore, we allocate the slots according to the CPU utilization of each task, which is defined as
div.formula: uci = CL 0 i + CL 1 i + • • • + CL m i -1 i Ti .(10)
div.p: To ensure the slot allocation matches the CPU utilization rate of each task, we define a penalty function:
Pi(wi, S) := max{-log wi/S uci , 0}.

When the slots assigned to a task are lower than its utilization rate, it incurs a penalty. Conversely, assigning too many slots to a task can hinder the scheduling of other tasks. Therefore, the penalty is set to be non-positive, avoiding any bonus points.

To address question 2 , we observe that the slot allocation process can be treated as a Knapsack problem, allowing for the application of dynamic programming (DP). Such a Knapsack problem is constructed as follows:

• Assigning w i slots to task τ i represents putting w i items into the Knapsack, with a total penalty of P i (w i , S); • w i should be at least 1 and no larger than the scheduling window S and the maximum workload length max i,j CL j i , denoted as CL max ; • The scheduling window size S times the number of CPUs N CP U is the Knapsack volume; • The algorithm needs to determine the best window size S and the optimal assignment to minimize the total penalty. The procedure of solving timeslot allocation by dynamic programming is detailed in Algo. 1, where Lines 8-14 handle the dynamic programming process, and Lines 16-22 retrieve the solutions and update the minimum penalty. We let dp[j] represent the minimum penalty achieved under the constraint
div.formula: w 0 + w 1 • • • + w n-1 ≤ j. Given a fixed scheduling window S, the total penalty is stored in dp[S × N CP U ].
div.p: After allocating the optimal slots for each task using the DP and applying Corollary IV.3.1, we re-evaluate the schedulability under the same benchmark and observe significant improvements. As shown in Fig. 4, when compared to the fair allocation, on a computing platform with 1 CPU and several PEs, the area under the curve improves by 36.5%; with 2 CPUs, the area growth extends to 59.6%, and the maximum utilization at the 100% schedulable ratio is doubled. Note that the slot assignment may be achieved with other evaluation metrics and heuristic algorithms, and we choose dynamic programming due to its simple implementation and low time complexity.

div.head: C. Scheduling and Response Time of PE Workloads
div.p: The PE workload is released to the accelerator after the previous CPU workload in the task is finished. This paper, without loss of generality, focuses on accelerators capable of handling multiple task partitions, as supported by commercial products like NVIDIA's Ampere architecture [29] and FPGA IP cores [28]. After the compiling and resource mapping performed by the compiler [44], [46], the PE workloads from n tasks are allocated to the accelerator with N P E PEs.

As an example, we allocate N P Ei amounts of dedicated PEs to each task τ i , such that its PE workload P L j i is ready immediately after the completion of the corresponding CPU workload CL j i . When it is a complete partition, tasks are allocated to their own PEs and do not need to compete for PEs, so there is no blocking time on the non-preemptive PEs. Therefore, the interference between PE workloads from different tasks is minimized, and the response time of PE workloads P R j i is equal to the execution time P T j i . Here, for a given partition, we can easily extend the formula Eqn. (3) to obtain the following Lemma IV.4 for calculating the response time P R j i of a PE workload P L j i . Lemma IV.4 Response time for PE workloads
div.formula: P R j i = P T j i = P L j i 1 -p j i + NP E i × p j i ,(12)
div.p: where p j i is the proportion of the parallel part of the PE workload.
PROOF. 5 Since the PEs are dedicatedly partitioned to each task without competition at runtime, for a PE workload, its response time P R j i is the execution time P T j i . □

In the example, we assumed the PEs are fully partitioned, leveraging approaches like brute-force searching for identifying the optimal partitioning. The approach still works for queue-based PE accessing manner, once the response time for each workload can be obtained [23]. The proposed method only requires the response time for each PE workload as inputs. Since no unique tricks are used in handling PE workloads, this method is compatible with most mainstream accelerators.

div.head: D. Building up the Scheduling Approach
div.p: We systematically outline the scheduling approach illustrated in Fig. 5. Our analysis begins with profiling tasks into the 3-tuple τ i as described in Eqn. (2). Then, we calculate the CPU and PE workload response time separately, as detailed in Sec. IV-B and Sec. IV-C. Finally, we analyze the timing and scheduling of the entire system offline. By applying Theorem IV.5, we can find at least one feasible scheduling arrangement 3 . The timeslot allocation result is then deployed to the online scheduler, which will be illustrated in Sec. V. In a real system, a task workload may finish earlier, allowing the slice it occupies to be taken by subsequent tasks. Consequently, the actual response time will be shorter than our analysis suggests.

Theorem IV.5 Given the slots allocation (w 0 , w 1 , . . . , w n-1 ), there exists at least one feasible assignments on N CP U CPUs (as shown in Fig. 2b), such that no task is assigned to two processors simultaneously. div.head: V. PRACTICAL SCHEDULER IN OPERATING SYSTEMS
div.p: To support the fine-grained timeslot allocation strategy proposed in Sec. IV, this section presents the scheduler design during system runtime.

div.head: A. Open-Loop Scheduler
div.p: Based on the scheduling strategy in Sec. IV, we start with a basic open-loop control scheduler for practical systems, named as TAG: timeslot allocation with user-definable granularity. The detailed flow is demonstrated in Algo. 2. In one scheduling window S, we maintain a priority queue of tasks based on the remaining slot number w i (Line 3). In each round, the scheduler schedules N CP U tasks with most slots and deducts one slot from them (Lines 5-8). The scheduler performs scheduling at regular intervals, which is user-definable and named as control granularity g (Line 9). After completing one scheduling window S, the slots are reset to initial values (Lines 10-12). Note that the scheduling windows S is an integer multiple of the control granularity g.

div.head: B. Closed-Loop Scheduler with Time-Tracer Module
div.p: Despite the straightforward principle and ease of implementation of the open-loop control scheduler, it cannot guarantee the scheduling performance. Unlike the scheduling in homogeneous systems, tasks in accelerator-enabled systems frequently suspend themselves (because of the segmented execution pattern) and enter "sleep" mode from the operating system's perspective. However, the open-loop control scheduler only updates priorities at fixed intervals, during which important tasks may be suspended and may not be assigned an optimal priority when they are ready for CPU computing.

To address this, we enhance the scheduler to be closedloop controlled, and tailored to the segmented characteristics of tasks. This improvement allows the scheduler to obtain the task's execution status and make more balanced decisions. We again face two major questions: 1 In Linux systems, where can we get the execution time of the tasks and the corresponding precision? 2 How should our scheduler make priority adjustments based on the execution status of the tasks?

For question 1 , the process CPU time is exposed in /proc/pid/stat/ for each process and /proc/ pid/task/tid/stat/ for each thread. This interface provides the time that process/thread has been scheduled in both user and kernel mode, measured in user space clock ticks [52]. But the timing precision (resolution) is only 10 ms.

To improve the timing precision to sub ms scale, we implement a task CPU time tracing kernel module. We mainly create two /proc entries for communication between user space applications and the kernel. The first entry, /proc/trace_pid, accepts input from the user space and records the PID to be monitored. The second entry, /proc/trace, exposes the execution time of each thread by task_cputime_adjusted() function from the kernel libraries to provide kernel tick-based CPU time accounting.

For question 2 , based on the open-loop scheduler in Algo. 2, we refine Lines 3 and 7. At regular time intervals (control granularity), the scheduler reads from our kernel module and updates the elapsed CPU time t i for each task since the last read. The priorities are fine-tuned as follows:
1) Initialize w i with w i + λw i , where λ is the reciprocal of the scheduling window (i.e., λ = 1/S) 2) Update w i by
div.formula: w i0 = w i0 -1 + λ(w ′ i0 -t i0 )
div.p: , where w ′ i0 is the initial slot value. 3) After completing one scheduling window, the priority tuple (w 0 , . . . , w n-1 ) resets to the initial slot allocation.

This adjustment results in an accurate priority assignment due to the inclusion of recent CPU time. The scaling factor λ ensures that λ(w ′ i0 -t i0 ) is always smaller than 1, maintaining the dominance of w i0 . Therefore, in each round the assigned tasks (such as τ 0 and τ 2 in Fig. 6b are reserved with the highest priority as in the HRT analysis, ensuring the theoretical response time (schedulability) in Sec. IV. If an assigned task is not yet ready, priority is given to tasks with less CPU usage within the same scheduling window, favoring tasks that have just finished their PE workloads and are offloading to CPUs. Fig. 7 illustrates the structure of the TAG scheduler, consisting of a task scheduler and a CPU time tracing kernel module. The scheduling starts by 1 ⃝ writing the application process ID into the /proc entry, allowing it to be recorded by the kernel module. Then at regular intervals, defined by the control granularity g, the task scheduler initiates a request 2 ⃝ to obtain CPU time for each thread by invoking the open() system call on the trace entry. This triggers the tracing function, which 3 ⃝ reads the accumulated CPU time from kernel libraries and exposes it in /proc entry. In the space, the task scheduler then computes the elapsed CPU time for each task, updates the corresponding priority 4 ⃝, and schedules the tasks accordingly 5 ⃝. This closed-loop scheduler operates following the procedure outlined in Algo. 2, with modifications to Lines 8 and 9 to reflect the above interactions. The choice of control granularity g significantly impacts scheduling performance, as examined through extensive experiments in Sec. VI to determine its optimal setting.

div.head: C. Scheduler Overhead and Frequency
div.p: The proposed scheduling module is invoked every g ms. The average cost for reading from the kernel module, sorting the priority queue, and setting thread priority is 6.33 µs. On the same machine, the classic Global-EDF scheduler's overhead is 5.03 µs. The EDF scheduler is invoked with each new job release, making it to the number of tasks and workload lengths. If the number of tasks doubles and the average workload length halves, the frequency increases fourfold. In contrast, the proposed scheduling makes scheduling decisions at regular and user-defined intervals, independent of tasksets.

div.head: VI. EVALUATION
div.p: In this section, we evaluate the proposed HARD with both numerical simulations and experiments on general-purpose heterogeneous computing platforms equipped with multiple CPU cores and accelerator PEs.

div.head: A. HRT (Response Time Analysis) Schedulability
div.p: The HRT performance is evaluated by the theoretically guaranteed schedulability derived from the proposed response time analysis approaches given the corresponding scheduler.
1) Response Time Analysis Approaches: We compare the performance of the following state-of-the-art response time analysis algorithms:

• HRT Performance (Response Time Analysis) for Global EDF-Like scheduler: This approach [7] targets accelerator-enabled architecture with single CPU core, under Global EDF-Like (GEL) scheduling, offering superior schedulability. • HRT Performance (Response Time Analysis) for Rate-Monotonic scheduler: These approaches are respectively designed for accelerator-enabled architecture with a single core (SelfS [53]) and multiple core CPUs (SHAPE [9]), under Rate-Monotonic Scheduling. • HRT Performance (Response Time Analysis) for HARD scheduler: Our proposed approach for analyzing accelerator-enabled architectures with multiple core CPUs and many PE accelerators. 2) Task Generation: To evaluate the schedulability of the proposed approaches under various configurations, we measure the schedulable ratio at targeted utilization levels. The schedulable ratio for a given utilization level is defined as the number of schedulable task sets divided by the total number of task sets generated for that level. The utilization level, denoted as u (plotted on the x-axis), represents the total system utilization, calculated as the sum of individual task utilizations:

For fair and consistent comparisons, we adopt methodologies similar to those in prior works [4], [9], [54] to generate the lengths of CPU and processing element (PE) workloads. These lengths are randomly sampled from a uniform distribution within the range of [1,10] ms. The deadline D i of task i is set based on the generated workload lengths and its utilization rate:
div.formula: D i = ( mi-1 j=0 CL j i +
div.p: mi-2 j=0 P L j i )/u i , where CL j i and P L j i represent the CPU and PE workload lengths, respectively. default computing platform has CPU cores, 10 PEs, and 5 parallel tasks running. Since EDF-Like [7] and SelfS [53] do not support multiple CPU platforms, we divide the 5 tasks into 2 separate groups following the consideration of their utilization sum is nearest and run 2 tests separately.

3) Comparison with HRT Response Time Analysis: To compare the schedulability of different approaches, we measure the maximum task set utilization concerning a given schedulable ratio goal in each of the three approaches. We mainly examined three parameters:

• Task number n (Fig. 8a to Fig. 8c): As the number of tasks increases from 5 to 9, all methods improve their schedulability except for the self-suspension method. In the default setting, HARD maintains 100% schedulable when the u ≤ 1.6, while other methods drop below 1.3. Measuring at the 0% schedulable rate, HARD shows similar performance to EDF-Like. When n = 9, HARD outperforms the other methods significantly. • Workload number m (Fig. 8a, 8d, 8e and 8f): As the workload number in each task increases, overall performance trends similarly to the increase in n. This indicates that the HRT performance of HARD is not significantly impacted by the workload number m. We applied a near-optimal partition strategy for EDF-L, chances are that two groups are perfectly averaged. Other scheduling algorithms can also benefit from this partitioning strategy and perform better at the tail. • CPU: PE workload ratio (Fig. 8g to Fig. 8i): Considering varying workloads on CPUs and PEs, we test these approaches with different CPU and PE workload lengths. For example, "CPU:PE workload 1 : 5" means CPU workloads vary from 1 to 10, while PE workloads vary from 1 to 50. Under the premise of similar overall scheduling performance, HARD achieves the highest schedulability at 100% and shows resilience to variations in CPU and PE workloads.

div.head: B. Average Measured Schedulability
div.p: The AMS performance is evaluated based on the schedulability from runtime measurements on a real system scheduled by the proposed scheduler.
1) Scheduling Approaches: We compare the performance of the following prevalent real-system scheduling algorithms:

• Global EDF-Like Scheduler (analyzed by [7]): This method assigns priorities based on task deadlines and adjusts priorities when a new job is released. • Rate-Monotonic Scheduler (analyzed by [4], [9], [53]):

This approach fixes thread priorities to values (such as 99, 98, and so on) using pthread_setschedparam throughout the test. • HARD Scheduler (analyzed by Corollary IV.3.1 and Lemma IV.4): This is our proposed method using the TAG scheduler shown in Fig. 7.

2) System Implementation: Our hardware platform consists of an Intel i7-10900X CPU and an NVIDIA RTX 3080 GPU. The software environment includes Ubuntu 22.04 Desktop with kernel 5.19.0 and CUDA 12.0, with a kernel tick frequency of 250 Hz. We implement persistent threads [42], [55] to support the partitioning of PEs (i.e., SMs in GPUs). Each persistent thread block links multiple thread blocks of one PE workload and is assigned to the SMs for the entire execution lifetime of the PE workload. The whole program creates 5 task threads to reduce context switch expenses, plus a scheduler thread. Each task thread performs FP32 matrix additions and multiplications as determined by the workload length.
3) Comparison with Scheduling Approaches: We test the system schedulability as overall utilization increases. We examine HARD with two primary parameters:

• Taskset Unit: We perform the same scheduling tests with task unit lengths of 1 ms and 10 ms, respectively. For example, if CL j i = 3, then under a 10 ms-unit taskset, the amount of floating-point calculation is scaled to compute for 30 ms. Comparing Fig. 9e with Fig. 9c, where both g = 1 ms, shows that HARD's performance improves with 10 ms-unit tasksets due to the overhead of changing priorities being more negligible. These results also demonstrate HARD's scalability to longer tasksets. the other two schedulers at a schedulable ratio higher than 80%. However, when u > 2.4, due to the overhead of frequent priority inversion (affecting both HARD and EDF), the Rate-Monotonic scheduler performs best.

div.head: C. Using HARD on AI Neural Networks
div.p: We use the proposed HARD scheduler to manage real AI workloads, for example, classic neural networks (NN), and compared its HRT and AMS schedulability against state-ofthe-art scheduling and response time analysis approaches. For this evaluation, we employed five tasks, each representing a neural network with 4 to 10 layers and 1024 neurons per layer, running on the two systems with one and two accelerators. The first system is the same as Sec. VI-B2, while the second system features one more NVIDIA GTX 1660Super GPU, to study the capability of selected approaches under multiaccelerator systems. The execution times on CPUs and PEs are measured before deployment. Deadlines and periods were generated using the method outlined in Sec. VI-A2. Fig. 10 illustrates the schedulability curve under neural network workloads, comparing the analytic results and system performance across the three scheduling methods, with a control granularity g = 100 µs. The HARD scheduler exhibited the best performance for both criterias, particularly at the 100% schedulable ratio. Measuring by the area under the curve, it improved hard real-time schedulability by 11.3% and average measured performance by 2.9%. Additionally, HARD significantly reduced pessimism (the gap between AMS and HRT) by 45.1%, "pushing" the HRT (theoretical response time analysis) closer to the measurements on the real system. Fig. 11 shows the schedulability under a two-accelerator system, and HARD still outperforms other methods in the HRT part. It's worth noting that all the methods exhibit less analytic pessimism, this is because we dedicate the tasks to specific accelerators and thus the resource competition between the parallel tasks is loosed.

Conclusively, for the HRT part, the HARD scheduler reaches the maximum utilization when measuring at 100% schedulable ratio, improving up to 25.0%. Comparing the AMS, HARD performs better at finer control granularity and outperforms the others at a schedulable ratio higher than 80%. HARD is also readily applicable to real AI workloads, improving schedulability significantly.

div.head: VII. CONCLUSION
div.p: This work presents HARD, a comprehensive real-time scheduling framework designed to enhance the scheduling and analysis of parallel tasks on accelerator-enabled computing architectures. HARD integrates an operating system scheduler with a response time analysis based on a timeslot allocation scheduling strategy. HARD leverages the subtask-level dynamicity of tasks to achieve improved schedulability. To support its scheduling algorithm, HARD introduces the TAG runtime scheduler, which operates under closed-loop control with a fine-grained time-tracing kernel module, allowing userdefined granularity. Compared to state-of-the-art scheduling approaches, HARD is evaluated through both schedulability analysis and real-system experiments. Results demonstrate significant improvements in schedulability, particularly for systems with stringent hard real-time (HRT) requirements. Notably, when applied to scheduling neural network workloads, HARD achieves up to a 27.3% improvement in HRT schedulability.
